relevance_reason: Reports patients from two families with biallelic COL3A1 variants, polymicrogyria and connective tissue features, which is the subject of this entry.

findings.statement: Horn et al. (2017) described a 3-year-old girl with developmental delay who was born with bilateral clubfoot, joint laxity, and dysmorphic facial features. At age 2 years she had an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage. Cerebral MRI showed a distinctive pattern of profound cerebral abnormalities, including bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone type.
quotes: In a 3-year-old female with developmental delay the nonsense variant c.1282C>T, p.(Arg428*) was detected
This patient was born with bilateral clubfoot, joint laxity, and dysmorphic facial features. At the age of 2 years she developed an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage.
Cerebral MRI showed a peculiar pattern of profound cerebral abnormalities including bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone variant.

findings.statement: In the 3-year-old girl with polymicrogyria and connective tissue features, Horn et al. (2017) identified compound heterozygous COL3A1 variants: a nonsense variant, c.1282C>T (p.Arg428Ter), and a frameshift variant, c.2057delC (p.Pro686LeufsTer105). Both variants were novel.
quotes: In a 3-year-old female with developmental delay the nonsense variant c.1282C>T, p.(Arg428*) was detected in combination the c.2057delC, p.(Pro686Leufs*105) frame shift variant. Both compound heterozygous variants were novel.

findings.statement: Horn et al. (2017) described a second family in which 2 affected sibs had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, white matter abnormalities, developmental delay, and seizures.
quotes: In the second family, the two affected siblings were homozygous for the missense variant c.145C<G, p.(Pro49Ala) of COL3A1 and showed cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, and white matter abnormalities, developmental delay, and seizures.

findings.statement: In 2 sibs with cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, and seizures, Horn et al. (2017) identified a homozygous missense variant in COL3A1, reported as c.145C<G (p.Pro49Ala).
quotes: In the second family, the two affected siblings were homozygous for the missense variant c.145C<G, p.(Pro49Ala) of COL3A1

findings.statement: Horn et al. (2017) noted that 3 more families had previously been reported with biallelic COL3A1 variants. All had specific structural brain anomalies, and some had a severe Ehlers-Danlos syndrome phenotype. The brain phenotype was characterized by bilateral frontoparietal cobblestone polymicrogyria, cerebellar microcysts, and white matter abnormalities, and it resembled the neurologic features of patients with autosomal recessive GPR56 mutations.
quotes: To date, three further families have been reported with biallelic variants of this gene and specific structural brain anomalies in all, and a severe Ehlers-Danlos syndrome phenotype in some.

Bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone variant, cerebellar microcysts, and abnormalities of the white matter characterize this brain phenotype and resemble neurological manifestations in individuals with autosomal recessive mutations in GPR56

findings.statement: Horn et al. (2017) noted that GPR56 acts as a ligand of COL3A1. Consistent with findings in knockout mice, they concluded that collagen III helps regulate cortical development as well as connective tissue formation.
quotes: GPR56, which serves as a ligand of COL3A1

In concordance with the findings in knock out mice, the collagen III protein plays a role in the regulation of cortical development in addition to its well-known function in connective tissue formation.

relevance_reason: Reports a family with a homozygous COL3A1 variant and reviews prior bi-allelic COL3A1 cases with cobblestone-like cortical malformation (polymicrogyria-like), white matter changes and cerebellar cysts.

findings.statement: Vandervore et al. (2017) reported a family with 2 affected and 2 unaffected sibs in which brain MRI of the affected sibs, as well as of 2 previously reported individuals with bi-allelic COL3A1 mutations, showed a brain phenotype similar to that associated with GPR56 mutations: cobblestone-like cortical malformation, white matter changes, and cerebellar cysts. The authors noted variability of the phenotype across patients.
quotes: Exome analysis was performed in a family consisting of two affected and two non-affected siblings. Brain imaging studies of this family and of two previously reported individuals with bi-allelic mutations in COL3A1 were reviewed.
Brain MRI in the affected siblings as well as in the two previously reported individuals with bi-allelic COL3A1 mutations showed a brain phenotype similar to that associated with mutations in GPR56.

findings.statement: In 2 sibs with cobblestone-like cortical malformation, white matter changes and cerebellar cysts, Vandervore et al. (2017) identified by exome analysis a novel homozygous variant, c.145C>G (p.Pro49Ala), in exon 2 of the COL3A1 gene. Functional assays were performed on dermal fibroblasts.
quotes: Exome analysis revealed a novel homozygous variant c.145C>G (p.Pro49Ala) in exon 2 of COL3A1.
Functional assays were performed on dermal fibroblasts.

findings.statement: Vandervore et al. (2017) concluded that homozygous or compound heterozygous COL3A1 mutations were associated with cobblestone-like malformation in all 3 families reported to date, and suggested that the phenotypic variability indicates that alterations in distinct domains of type III procollagen can lead to different outcomes.
quotes: Homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in COL3A1 are associated with cobblestone-like malformation in all three families reported to date.
The variability of the phenotype across patients suggests that genetic alterations in distinct domains of type III procollagen can lead to different outcomes.

findings.statement: Vandervore et al. (2017) noted that type III procollagen is the ligand of GPR56 (ADGRG1) and that the presence of cobblestone-like malformation in patients with bi-allelic COL3A1 mutations emphasized the critical role of the type III collagen-GPR56 axis and the pial membrane in brain development and cortical lamination.
quotes: Type III procollagen, the chains of which are encoded by COL3A1, is the ligand of the G protein-coupled receptor 56 (GPR56), also known as adhesion G protein-coupled receptor G1.

The presence of cobblestone-like malformation in patients with bi-allelic COL3A1 mutations emphasises the critical role of the type III collagen-GPR56 axis and the pial membrane in the regulation of brain development and cortical lamination.

relevance_reason: Reports siblings with biallelic COL3A1 variants, vascular EDS, and frontoparietal polymicrogyria in the sister. This is a defining family for the polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type EDS phenotype.

findings.statement: Jørgensen et al. (2015) described a boy (III-2) who was born with right-sided clubfoot and had a unilateral testicular hydrocele, crowded teeth, retrognathia, long slender fingers, and pale translucent skin. He died unexpectedly at age 15 years after a week of backache. Autopsy showed dissections of the thoracic aorta, the right renal artery and the left femoral artery, with extensive bleeding and cystic medial necrosis of the aortic wall. The brain looked macroscopically normal, but neither brain imaging nor histological cerebral examination was performed.
quotes: The proband was born with right-sided clubfoot and developed unilateral hydrocele of the testis

Autopsy revealed three dissections: a transverse dissection including nearly the whole circumference of the thoracic aorta at the level of ligamentum arteriosus, and separate dissections of the right renal artery and the left femoral artery.
The brain had normal macroscopic appearance, and cerebral dissection at autopsy revealed no obvious macroscopic anomalies. Neither brain imaging nor histological cerebral examinations were performed.

findings.statement: Jørgensen et al. (2015) described the proband's sister (III-3). She had long slender fingers, small-joint hypermobility, translucent skin with visible veins, the facial features of vascular EDS, spontaneous rupture of small superficial vessels, intermittent abdominal pain with blood in the stool, and migraine with aura. By age 19 to 20 years she had dissections of both internal carotid arteries and a stenosis of the right external iliac artery, while aortic dimensions were normal. Brain MRI showed bilateral thickened frontoparietal cortices with small gyri, consistent with pachy-micropolygyria. Despite this, her cognition was normal, her neurologic examination was normal, she had never had seizures, and her motor and language development had been normal.
quotes: She had cerebral cortical dysplasia with thickened frontoparietal cortices bilaterally, small gyri and findings consistent with pachy micropolygyria (Figures 1c and d). She had normal cognitive functioning, a recent neurological examination was normal and she had not experienced epileptic seizures.
MR arteriography (Figure 1a) and CT angiography revealed a stenotic process in her right internal carotid (ICA) and ultrasonography of neck vessels proved to represent a dissection (data not shown).

The siblings III-2 and III-3 both manifested pale, translucent skin with visible subcutaneous vessels and facial features characteristic of EDS type IV with a small lower jaw, prominent eyes, pinched nose, and thin upper lip.

findings.statement: Jørgensen et al. (2015) found that both affected sibs were compound heterozygous for 2 COL3A1 variants. One was a nonsense variant, c.1786C>T (p.Arg596Ter), in exon 26, which encodes part of the triple helical domain. They inherited it from their father, who was clinically unaffected at age 63. The proband had no variants in FBN1, TGFBR1, or TGFBR2. The unaffected brother carried neither COL3A1 variant.
quotes: The proband (III-2) and his sister (III-3) were each heterozygous for two COL3A1 sequence variants: c.1786C>T, p.(Arg596*) in exon 26, which encodes part of the triple helical domain of proα1(III)

the father (II-5) was heterozygous for the COL3A1 c.1786C>T, p.(Arg596*) sequence variant, which confirmed that the variants were in trans. The unaffected brother (III-1) of the proband had neither variant.

findings.statement: Jørgensen et al. (2015) found that the second COL3A1 variant in the affected sibs was a missense variant, c.3851G>A (p.Gly1284Glu), in exon 50, which encodes part of the C-terminal propeptide. The sibs inherited it from their mother, who had only partial features of the disorder. The substituted glycine is highly conserved and lies next to a cysteine involved in interchain disulfide bonding, within a calcium-binding region. The authors predicted that the change would slow assembly of the trimer.
quotes: c.3851G>A, p.(Gly1284Glu) in exon 50, which encodes a portion of the carboxyl-terminal propeptide
The mother (II-6) was heterozygous for the COL3A1 c.3851G>A, p.(Gly1284Glu) sequence variant

Substitution of glycine by glutamic acid at position 1284 of the proα1(III) chain (p.Gly1284Glu) predicts the change of a highly conserved amino acid that is adjacent to the one of two cysteine residues involved in interchain, intramolecular disulfide bond formation

findings.statement: Jørgensen et al. (2015) studied cultured dermal fibroblasts. Cells from the compound heterozygous sister made a reduced amount of type III procollagen, and all of its chains had abnormal electrophoretic mobility, consistent with overmodification. Cells from the mother (missense heterozygote) made mostly normal type III procollagen plus a small amount of slightly overmodified procollagen. Cells from the father (nonsense heterozygote) made a reduced amount of apparently normal type III procollagen.
quotes: Cultured dermal fibroblasts from III-3 produced a reduced amount of type III procollagen, the chains of which all had an abnormal electrophoretic mobility (Figure 2b).

Dermal fibroblasts from II-6, heterozygous for the missense mutation, produced mostly normal and a small amount of abnormal type III procollagen in which there was subtle overmodification of the chains.
Dermal fibroblasts from II-5 heterozygous for the nonsense mutation produced a reduced amount of apparently normal type III procollagen.

findings.statement: Jørgensen et al. (2015) reported marked clinical variation within the family. The father and other paternal relatives who were heterozygous for the nonsense variant had no complications or clinical features of vascular EDS; the paternal grandmother was healthy at 85 years. The mother, heterozygous for the missense variant, had thin skin with visible vessels, reduced elasticity of the ascending aorta, and emphysema, but not the full vascular EDS phenotype by age 60. The authors concluded that biallelic variants give a significantly worse outcome than heterozygous variants.
quotes: None of the individuals with the variant in the father's family had complications or clinical features consistent with the diagnosis of vEDS.
the father (c.1786C>T, p.(Arg596*)) did not have abnormal clinical findings at age 63 and the mother (c.3851G>A, p.(Gly1284Glu)) did not express a complete picture of vascular-type EDS by age 60.

Biallelic sequence variants have a significantly worse outcome than heterozygous variants for either null mutations or missense mutations, and frontoparietal polymicrogyria may be an added phenotype feature.

findings.statement: Jørgensen et al. (2015) noted that type III collagen is the ligand for GPR56, and that GPR56 variants cause recessive bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria. They suggested that the GPR56–type III collagen interaction forms part of a pathway in brain formation, and they proposed a novel syndromic recessive form of vascular EDS that combines tissue fragility with cerebrocortical anomalies. They also acknowledged that the brain findings could be coincidental or caused by variants in a second gene.
quotes: Our clinical findings and those described by Plancke et al suggest that the interaction of GPR56 and type III (pro)collagen identifies two parts of a pathway involved in frontotemporal brain formation.
suggests that a novel syndromic form of recessively inherited vascular Ehlers–Danlos includes both tissue fragility and cerebrocortical anomalies.
we recognize that the two phenotypes could reflect the presence of variants in a second gene

relevance_reason: Mouse knockout study showing that losing Col3a1 causes a cobblestone-like cortical malformation. It supports the link between COL3A1 (collagen III, the GPR56 ligand) and brain malformation.

findings.statement: Jeong et al. (2012) found that Col3a1-null mice had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, with breakdown of the pial basement membrane (BM), neuronal overmigration, detachment of radial glial endfeet, and marginal zone heterotopias. All Col3a1-null mice examined at embryonic day (E) 18.5 had neuronal ectopias on the brain surface. These ectopias contained neurons from both deep and superficial cortical layers (Cux1+, Tbr1+, and CTIP2+), which mirrored Gpr56-null mice. Ectopia penetrance was 23 of 28 in null embryos, 0 of 12 in heterozygotes, and 0 of 20 in wildtype embryos.
quotes: We observed a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, with BM breakdown and marginal zone heterotopias in Col3a1⁻/⁻ mouse brains.

Neurons positive for Cux1, Tbr1 and CTIP2 were detected in the ectopias, suggesting that the ectopic cells in the Col3a1 −/− cortex were neurons from both deep and superficial cortical layers, mirroring our observations of Gpr56 null mutant mice

findings.statement: Jeong et al. (2012) found that in Col3a1-null mice the pial BM formed normally at E10.5, even though collagen III was absent. Regional breakdown of the BM, with neuronal overmigration, appeared in about half of E11.5 embryos and in all embryos older than E12.5. In the mutants, radial glial endfeet protruded through the breached BM, and Cajal-Retzius cells and calbindin-positive interneurons were misplaced into the ectopias.
quotes: Interestingly, in spite of the absence of collagen III, the pial BM was initially properly formed at E10.5 in the mutant mice (Figure 3J). Regional breakdown of the pial BM with concurrent neuronal overmigration was observed in about half of the E11.5 and all embryos older than E12.5 in the Col3a1 −/− brains analyzed
We observed protruded endfeet through a breached pial BM in some of the E11.5 and all of the E12.5 Col3a1 −/− brains
we observed misplaced CR cells beyond the defective BM in Col3a1 −/− brains

findings.statement: Jeong et al. (2012) found that meningeal fibroblasts from Col3a1-null mice had no obvious defects, and that the level of glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan in mutant brains was unchanged. They suggested that collagen III, the ligand of GPR56, regulates cortical development independently of the dystroglycan pathway, and that the dyslamination results from the absence of collagen III rather than from a defect in meningeal fibroblasts.
quotes: We failed to detect any change in the level of α-dystroglycan in the brains of Col3a1 −/− mice, arguing that the function of collagen III does not directly affect the expression and glycosylation of dystroglycan
This finding suggests that collagen III regulates cortical development independent of the dystroglycan pathway.
suggesting that the cortical dyslamination seen in Col3a1 −/− mice is not the direct result of cellular defects of MFs, but rather the absence of collagen III, the ligand of GPR56.

findings.statement: Jeong et al. (2012) noted that homozygous Col3a1 deletion mostly caused perinatal lethality, with only about 5% of mice surviving to adulthood. The survivors had features resembling vascular-type (type IV) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, including rupture of large blood vessels. Losing one allele caused no obvious defects. The authors postulated that biallelic COL3A1 mutations in humans may be associated with a lethal form of cobblestone lissencephaly similar to Walker-Warburg syndrome.
quotes: Col3a1 −/− usually results in perinatal lethality of an unknown etiology, with only 5% of mice reaching adulthood [16]. As for the surviving mice, their phenotype closely resembles the clinical manifestations of patients with type IV EDS, including the rupture of large blood vessels [16].
It is possible that mutations in both alleles of COL3A1 associate with a lethal form of cobblestone lissencephaly similar to WWS.

relevance_reason: Reports a homozygous COL3A1 null variant in a consanguineous girl with recessive vascular-type EDS, which directly characterises the autosomal recessive COL3A1 phenotype.

findings.statement: Plancke et al. (2009) studied a young girl with recessive Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. She was born to consanguineous, healthy parents and met the criteria for laboratory testing for vascular EDS.
quotes: Here, we study a case of recessive EDS in a young consanguineous girl of healthy parents. She fulfilled the vascular EDS criteria for laboratory testing.

findings.statement: Plancke et al. (2009) sequenced the entire COL3A1 cDNA of the proband and found a homozygous 1-bp duplication (c.479dupT) that causes a frameshift and a premature termination codon (p.Lys161GlnfsX45). Testing of genomic DNA showed that she inherited the variant from each of her parents.
quotes: Total sequencing of COL3A1 cDNA identified a homozygous nucleotide duplication (c.479dupT) resulting in a premature termination codon (p.Lys161GlnfsX45).
Studies in genomic DNA showed that this mutation was inherited from each parent.

findings.statement: In the proband, Plancke et al. (2009) used RT-PCR, quantitative PCR, immunohistochemistry and Western blot to study expression. They found strong mRNA decay and no type III collagen.
quotes: The expression analysis (RT-PCR, quantitative-PCR, immunohistochemistry, WB) showed strong mRNA decay and an absence of type III collagen in the proband.

findings.statement: Plancke et al. (2009) reported that the proband's heterozygous parents and other healthy relatives in earlier generations, who were expected to have COL3A1 haploinsufficiency, did not show features of vascular EDS. The authors suggested that COL3A1 haploinsufficiency has a stochastic effect in humans. They proposed this could be explained by how efficient nonsense-mediated mRNA decay is, and by the resulting dominant-negative effect, depending on where the mutation lies and/or on modifying factors.
quotes: The expected COL3A1 haploinsufficiency in her healthy ascendants did not lead to the manifestations of vascular EDS.

This case provides evidence of a stochastic effect of COL3A1 haploinsufficiency in humans, which could be explained by the relation between nonsense-mediated mRNA decay efficiency and the resulting dominant-negative effect depending on the position of the mutation and/or modifying factors.

relevance_reason: The paper reports COL3A1 null (premature termination) mutations causing a vascular EDS-like phenotype. This is relevant to the vascular-type EDS component of the COL3A1-related entry. Polymicrogyria is not mentioned in the abstract.

findings.statement: Schwarze et al. (2001) identified three heterozygous frameshift mutations in the COL3A1 gene (1832delAA, 413delC, and 555delT) in probands with a phenotype similar to vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. The mutations led to premature termination codons in exons 27, 6, and 9, respectively. The mRNA from each mutant allele was transcribed efficiently but rapidly degraded, presumably by nonsense-mediated decay, which made the allele product unstable.
quotes: We have now found three frameshift mutations (1832delAA, 413delC, and 555delT) that lead to premature termination codons (PTCs) in exons 27, 6, and 9, respectively, and to allele-product instability.
The mRNA from each mutant allele was transcribed efficiently but rapidly degraded, presumably by the mechanisms of nonsense-mediated decay.

findings.statement: In a fourth patient with a phenotype similar to vascular EDS, Schwarze et al. (2001) identified a point mutation in the final exon of the COL3A1 gene, 4294C-T, that produced a premature termination codon (Arg1432Ter). The mutant mRNA was stable, but it led to synthesis of a truncated protein that was not incorporated into mature type III procollagen molecules.
quotes: In a fourth patient, we identified a point mutation, in the final exon, that resulted in a PTC (4294C-->T [Arg1432Ter]).
In this last instance, the mRNA was stable but led to synthesis of a truncated protein that was not incorporated into mature type III procollagen molecules.

findings.statement: Schwarze et al. (2001) reported that in all 4 probands with COL3A1 haploinsufficiency mutations, the presenting feature was vascular aneurysm or rupture. The resulting phenotype overlapped with that of vascular EDS.
quotes: In all probands, the presenting feature was vascular aneurysm or rupture.
the phenotypes produced by these mutations in COL3A1 overlap with those of the vascular form of EDS

findings.statement: Schwarze et al. (2001) concluded that null mutations in COL3A1 produce phenotypes that overlap with vascular EDS. In COL1A1 and COL2A1, by contrast, null mutations produce milder phenotypes than mutations that alter protein sequence. The authors suggested that the major effect of many dominant mutations in the 'minor' collagen genes may be expressed through protein deficiency rather than through incorporation of structurally altered molecules into fibrils. They noted that mice heterozygous for Col3a1 null alleles have no identified phenotype.
quotes: Thus, in contrast to mutations in genes that encode the dominant protein of a tissue (e.g., COL1A1 and COL2A1), in which "null" mutations result in phenotypes milder than those caused by mutations that alter protein sequence, the phenotypes produced by these mutations in COL3A1 overlap with those of the vascular form of EDS.

This suggests that the major effect of many of these dominant mutations in the "minor" collagen genes may be expressed through protein deficiency rather than through incorporation of structurally altered molecules into fibrils.
Furthermore, mice heterozygous for Col3a1 "null" alleles have no identified phenotype.

relevance_reason: Col3a1 knockout mouse model recapitulating vascular rupture of vascular-type (type IV) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

findings.statement: Liu et al. (1997) inactivated the Col3a1 gene in mouse embryonic stem cells by homologous recombination and derived homozygous mutant mice from heterozygous intercrosses. About 10% of homozygous mutant mice survived to adulthood but had a much shorter life span than wildtype mice; the major cause of death was rupture of the major blood vessels, similar to patients with type IV Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Ultrastructural analysis of mutant tissues showed that type III collagen is essential for normal collagen I fibrillogenesis in the cardiovascular system and other organs.
quotes: we have inactivated the Col3a1 gene in embryonic stem cells by homologous recombination
About 10% of the homozygous mutant animals survived to adulthood but have a much shorter life span compared with wild-type mice.
The major cause of death of mutant mice was rupture of the major blood vessels, similar to patients with type IV Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
